title: Thoughts From Dr. Joe: To right the unrightable wrong
text:
As a boy, I wasn't much of a joiner. Although I knew many kids, I never aligned myself to one particular group. But as I think back 47 years I remember running with a bunch of guys from the gym where I boxed.
We formed a club called The Knights. Many of our adventures on the mean streets of the Bronx evolved from that club. Denny Malvey was our boxing coach. In 1913 he beat Gene Tunney in a street fight in Hell's Kitchen on the Lower Westside. However, we were most impressed by his knowledge of King Arthur and The Knights of the Round Table. Denny introduced us to Sir Thomas Mallory's "Le Morte d'Arthur," and told us about the Arthurian Code of Chivalry.
"Lads," he'd say in his Irish brogue, "It's your duty to protect those who cannot protect themselves."
The reason Denny fought Gene Tunney, who eventually beat Jack Dempsey for the heavyweight championship was that Tunney was a bully who picked on the younger kids.
Denny was our idol. You knew what he stood for; we wanted to be like him. We were gifted fighters, and like Don Quixote followed the Arthurian code "To right the unrightable wrong." So we took on every bully from 241st to Gun Hill Road.
The scars on my face account for numerous altercations that I've had defending others and myself against bullies. However, as a young adult, I learned different skills counseling street gangs in the South Bronx.
Last week I wrote about Back to School Night at LCHS. I ended the write commenting on Ms. Baldwin's admonitions regarding the potential of bullying.
Five years ago I addressed this issue in a write called, "Mean Girls." My words resonated with many as I received numerous e-mails from readers commenting on their nightmarish memories when they were bullied as children. Many expressed how this brutalization left an indelible wound and led to a downward spiral adversely affecting their self-worth.
The handprints of bullies are like a slap on the face and remain stark and defined on the souls of their victims.
The newspapers tell stories of children who have taken their lives as a result of bullies. Phoebe Prince, Asher Brown, Eric Mohat and Sladjana Vidovic are the latest victims.
Where have we been? And I say this because according to Eldridge Cleaver, "If we're not part of the solution we're part of the problem." Why do we allow bullies to steal the souls of our children? Until one is committed to the cause, there is hesitancy/ Thus nothing is done and subsequently another child takes their life on our watch.
Some of our best minds struggle with modalities of prevention, accountability and therapeutic intervention. Many school districts have such paradigms. But it's not good enough! I would rather have a resolute commitment to end this form of slavery because someone who is resolute will find a way. Bullies thrive where authority is weak!
"Bullying is just a part of growing-up," some say. It's not! Although children are born very demanding, why haven't their parents socialized them?
In 1963 my buddies and I made a commitment that we would show no quarter to those who would terrorize another. We were the Knights and we were resolute! Instead of more institutionalized programs we need to be out brother's keeper. John Donne says, "No man is an island, entire of itself. …when the bells tolls for another, it tolls for thee."
The solution lies within us. The power of love, and attention is a prevailing intervention. But, we must be willing to bring hell down from heaven to put a stop to bullying.
My dear reader, it's time to become a Knight and join the ranks of Joey, Blasé, Tony and I, and right the unrightable wrong." That's what Knights do!
Are you in?
JOE PUGLIA is a practicing counselor, a professor of education at Glendale Community College and a former officer in the Marines. Reach him at doctorjoe@ymail.com.
summary: As a boy, I wasn't much of a joiner. Although I knew many kids, I never aligned myself to one particular group. But as I think back 47 years I remember running with a bunch of guys from the gym where I boxed.

title: Hudson County government to taxpayers: Be ready to pay more, says the Political Insider
text:
Your tax bill is divided into three parts -- schools, municipal, and county. Thursday evening, the Hudson County Board of Freeholders voted on a budget that decided one-third of your "l'addition."
Politically speaking, I'm always curious as to why freeholders approve a budget that guarantees a tax hike for their constituents.
Deciding what each municipality owes for county services is based on a semi-complicated formula. My understanding is that this recipe for blood-sucking takes into consideration factors such as property assessments in a municipality, and an equalization equation -- which this year shows a deficit for everyone except Guttenberg. Add to it the eye of a newt and, although heatedly denied, a pinch of politics.
The total tax levy for the county's municipalities in 2011 was $279.7 million. This year's sum is $291.1 million. This is an increase of $11.4 million, or a 4.1 percent jump over last year's budget.
The largest numerical tax levy increase is in Jersey City, with $48.6 million or a 4.5 percent hike over last year.
Communities that will see a decrease in collections are East Newark, $28,622 less, or 15 percent, and surprisingly, West New York and its tony waterfront, which will see a $420,037 drop in the tax burden, or 3.33 percent.
Other big money tax hikes are Hoboken again, $2.4 million, or 5.2 percent; Bayonne, $1.7 million, or 6.6 percent, and what has become a tradition, Union City, $1.1 million, or 6.7 percent.
Those are the nuts and bolts. Now for the interesting voters. Let's first say that Freeholders Bill O'Dea of Jersey City and Tilo Rivas of Union City voted "no." O'Dea always feels more could be cut from the spending plan, and Rivas is echoing the sentiments of his boss, Mayor and Sen. Brian Stack.
Why did Freeholders Eliu Rivera, board chairman, and Jeff Dublin, both of Jersey City, say yes to the budget and its increases?
Rivera was unavailable for comment, but Dublin said it allows for fair pay for county workers at a time when the economy affects people and governments. He said every effort was made to cut corners.
Freeholders Doreen DiDomenico of Bayonne and Anthony Romano of Hoboken echoed Dublin's comments about the county doing its best to pare down costs.
In Hoboken's case, there is the feeling by Mile Square City officials that the county administration has been more than fair to their city. For instance, county administration sources say the Hudson County Sheriff's Office is providing a great deal of policing because of reduced local manpower -- attrition, including retirements, according to sources. When the Lepre-Con event -- replacing the St. Patrick's Day parade -- was held, there were 100 sheriff's officers in Hoboken. They are expected to provide an equal number of officers on Independence Day.
Add to this all the work being done on the 14th Street viaduct, plans to construct park space under the viaduct, a number of street pavings and improvements, a return to the city of a couple of small county streets, and watch for some future work on Observer Highway. Hoboken also received $3 million from the county's Open Space Trust Fund, which may go with Mayor Dawn Zimmer's plan to use eminent domain to acquire land between Ninth and 14th streets. Doesn't that location sound like the vicinity of some big bus company?
Most all the freeholders agree that the big problem with putting together a budget is Jersey City, because the county seat has relied heavily on developing its waterfront with tax abatements. Only 5 percent of what is collected in lieu of taxes goes to the county and officials say they have to investigate whether or not the county is actually getting those funds. In essence, the other Hudson communities are subsidizing Jersey City's county services -- and development.
Every budget vote fuels the argument that Hudson could survive without county government. There are some municipal officials who believe they could exist with a county structure that only provides for health services, policing and the courts. In fact, some freeholders believe that sheriff's officers could also man municipal courts, freeing local police for other duties. And in an age of regionalization, there is some (very small) talk about eliminating all police in favor of a countywide metro police. Change comes at a snail's pace in this county.
In the end, all a constituent knows is that he or she is picking up the freight for another layer of government.
HOW IT ALL STACKS UP
It's been an interesting couple of weeks for Stack.
First he backs U.S. Rep. Bill Pascrell in the Democratic Party primary and the Passaic County pol pulls out the win for the 9th District over Congressman Steve Rothman of Englewood, who was supported by most of the Hudson County Democratic Organization.
On Tuesday, most Dem mayors and leaders are convinced that Stack helped save Bayonne Mayor Mark Smith's bacon by showing up with a busload of Union City party committee people at the HCDeadO's reorganization meeting to vote for Smith.
Most believe that a busload of North Bergen committee people sent by North Bergen Mayor and Sen. Nick Sacco were set to nominate Assemblyman Vincent Prieto of Secaucus for the chair and that would have given Sacco some statewide notoriety as a powerbroker and safeguard is already hefty patronage in county government.
I'm sure Sacco folks would say that was never on their mind. It's just that Stack never organizes a show of strength. It was also worth noting that Smith held up the reorganization meeting to give the Union City party committee bus time to finally arrive at what would be a 10-minute meeting. I just don't know why North Bergen didn't plan more alliances, if they were serious.
This means Smith pulled a Machiavellian fast one by sitting down with the HCDeadO's satan several weeks prior to the Tuesday reorganization. What was the deal with the devil? More than likely, the offer to the Union City boss was a guarantee that he will be on the HCDeadO line in the state senator's re-election effort next year. This would mean no civil war.
OK, let's see if Smith can withstand the pressure to back out of any such a deal.
Then on Thursday Stack held a small fund-raiser at the Waterside in North Bergen for about 300 people. You may remember the place as Frank's (Guarini) Waterside. The surprise here is that Jersey City Mayor Jerremiah Healy showed up and stayed a half-hour to make the rounds. No one can ever say Stack and Healy are drinking buddies. Stack doesn't drink.
Update: Made an error in this Insider note. I make mention of the Waterside catering and restaurant, above, but former Union City Mayor Arthur Wichert reminds me, and he's right, that the establishment was once connected to ex-Sen. Frank Lautenberg (Frank's Place) and not former congressman Frank Guarini. Thanks Artie.
I can't read much into this, except perhaps the Jersey City mayor wanted to upstage his rival, Downtown Councilman Steven Fulop, who was holding an event of his own that night at Zeppelin Hall Restaurant and Biergarten, where at $20 a ticket folks were entertained by a half-dozen bands and singers. You would have thought Healy would want to jump on the stage and belt out a few -- or just belt.
INSIDER NOTES
-- On Tuesday, former Assemblyman Lou Manzo, formerly of Jersey City and now living in Belmar, will speak at a Community Awareness Series session at the Miller Branch Library, 489 Bergen Ave., Jersey City.
You know what the subject is. It's Operation Bid Rig III. Manzo was arrested and indicted as a result of the federal sting, but Lou fought the law and won. Now it's payback time and Manzo will talk about federal justice and the U.S. Attorney's Office.
It's timely because of the flak Gov. Christie is receiving for some appointments to Monmouth County (Republican) government positions (prosecutor's office) for former members of the U.S. Attorney staff. Also there is talk about an old FBI report about informant Solomon Dwek's charges of corruption against past and present Monmouth County, as in GOP, officials. Last night, a "Reporter's Round Table" discussion on NJ TV was about Bid Rig criticism.
Gee, I could swear I wrote about much of this in past columns.
The Asbury Park Press came out with an editorial yesterday on the subject. In it the newspaper said:
"... former Monmouth County Sheriff Joseph Oxley, who was recently nominated by Gov. Chris Christie to become a Superior Court judge. The allegations are serious, and need to be addressed in a way devoid of politics. Dwek described himself as a "big fund-raiser" for Oxley, a former Middletown mayor who most recently served as Monmouth County's Republican chairman. He claims Oxley gave him a list of foreclosed properties to be auctioned off two weeks before it became public. This gives (Dwek) an opportunity to negotiate with the property owner before the auction and avoid competition and potentially higher prices," the FBI report stated ...
"The FBI said it found no wrongdoing in the matter, but one wonders whether politics may have played a part in the thoroughness (or lack thereof) of its investigation. Christie was the U.S. attorney at the time, and Oxley was a major player in the Republican Party in Monmouth County, which Christie often has credited with helping him win the governorship ..."
The Asbury Park Press suggests allowing Dwek to testify before the Senate Judiciary Committee during the Oxley confirmation hearing. I don't know. The FBI informant has already had problems testifying in court.
Manzo has been hurling these accusation before anyone else, which makes Tuesday's CAS event an entertainment special.
-- Hoboken City Council President Ravi Bhalla admitted that he was issued four tickets Tuesday morning after he allegedly made an improper turn at Washington Street and Observer Highway. He was socked with citations for making an improper turn at a traffic signal, driving with a suspended license, driving with an expired license, and not having a valid insurance card.
"Just pay the $2" is the the sage advice. Instead, Bhalla says he'll plead innocent to all complaints. he says the suspended license is nothing more then a miscommunication between New York and Garden State authorities. The councilman said New Jersey authorities did not receive information that he paid a parking ticket he received last September in New York City.
OK, but I believe that the law involving interstate agreements on traffic violations excludes parking tickets as a reason for suspending licenses.
So, what's the story Ravi?
-- The image of the week was a video of Mayors Dr. Felix Roque of West New York and Richard Turner of Weehawken sitting in the back of a West New York police pursuit vehicle, a Charger, trying to keep up with a pair of F1 star drivers in souped up Infiniti's at speeds reaching 95 to 100 mph.
Critics of the mayor can only wish they were in the back of the cop car for other reasons. In fact, when I was taking a video of Roque climbing into the car he said, "I bet you enjoy taking this picture." The West New York mayor faces federal charges of hacking an internet website calling for his recall. Turner is just annoying to some Dem leaders.
-- Happy Father's Day, including those who are up to date on their child support payments.
authors: Richard J. Mccormack For The Jersey Journal
Reena Rose Sibayan The Jersey Journal

title: TSX up: housing starts, Home Depot earns show further signs of housing rebound
text:
TORONTO – The Toronto stock market closed sharply higher Tuesday as a solid earnings report from the biggest U.S. home improvement retailer and a surge in housing starts reinforced sentiment that the American housing sector is rebounding.
The S&P/TSX composite index ran ahead 138.7 points to 15,477.17.
The Canadian dollar lost 0.48 of a cent to 91.38 cents US as the greenback strengthened following data that showed American housing starts surged 15.7 per cent in July to an annualized rate of 1.1 million units, the highest level in eight months. That came on the heels of a strong builders sentiment survey released Monday.
The Dow Jones industrials was ahead 80.85 points to 16,919.59, the Nasdaq was up 19.2 points to 4,527.51 and the S&P 500 index rose 9.86 points to 1,981.6.
“The construction data is very important because of jobs,” said Paul Taylor, chief investment officer, asset allocation, BMO Asset Management.
“The housing-related jobs have not really contributed over the last couple of years (to overall employment growth) and the fact that we’re at 1.1 million housing starts is a strong number. So housing is certainly no longer a headwind, it’s a strong tailwind and that’s an important factor.”
However, he added that it’s unlikely to persuade the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates earlier than generally expected, around mid-2015.
There was further positive news from the housing sector as Home Depot Inc. (NYSE:HD) reported its quarterly profit increased by 14 per cent to US$2.05 billion, or $1.52 per share, beating estimates by eight cents. The home-improvement retailer said revenue rose nearly six per cent to $23.81 billion, better than forecasts of $23.57 billion and its shares rose $4.64 or 5.55 per cent to US$88.23. Canadian rival Rona (TSX:RON) advanced 21 cents or 1.6 per cent to C$13.24 on the TSX.
Meanwhile, traders awaited possible guidance on the pace of interest rate increases by the U.S. Federal Reserve in 2015 when chairwoman Janet Yellen delivers the keynote address at the central bank’s annual meeting in Jackson Hole, Wyo. She is expected to again signal to the market that the central bank is in no rush to hike rates and when it does, the pace will be gradual.
Most TSX sectors were positive, led by a 1.85 per cent rise in the energy sector even as September crude dropped $1.93 to a seven-month low of US$94.48. Prices have plunged 10 per cent in the past month as it has become less likely that Islamic State insurgents would seriously impede Iraqi oil production.
The consumer staples sector was up 0.37 per cent with shares in Alimentation Couche-Tard (TSX:ATD.B) ahead 44 cents to C$31.33 after Reuters reported the Quebec-based retailer is among those shortlisted to buy a minority stake in China’s Sinopec Sales, the world’s largest fuel retail network. State-run Sinopec Sales is planning on selling a 30 per cent stake by the end of the year. The minority stake has an estimated value of US$16 billion.
The gold sector was down about 0.35 per cent as December bullion faded $2.60 to US$1,296.70 an ounce.
September copper was two cents lower at US$3.09 a pound and the base metals sector lost 0.32 per cent.

title: Minnehaha Co. Sheriff’s Office Sees ‘Cases And Cases’ Of Sexting In Schools: ‘It’s almost becoming problematic.’
text:
Following the arrest of an 18-year-old Baltic man this week, the Minnehaha County Sheriff’s Office is warning teenagers about the dangers of social media. The Sheriff’s Office says it’s not unusual for them to deal with extortion cases involving nude photos and teens.
“Be aware that it can be very harmful if you send pictures of yourself to somebody and they can use it for whatever they want,” said Minnehaha Co. Sheriff’s Office Capt. Jason Gearman.
The Sheriff’s Office says Nicholas Schmidt was arrested Wednesday thanks to a group of people who alerted authorities of a possible victim. They say they learned that the victim sent hundreds of nude photos to Schmidt over the course of the last year.
“This was the result it was kind of a disturbing trend that was going on and there may be more people out there that have encountered the same thing,” Gearman said.
According to an arrest affidavit, the 16-year-old girl told authorities that Schmidt would ask her to send him photos on SnapChat. Schmidt would get mad if she refused and would threaten to disperse the pictures of her at school. The affidavit says he also threatened to disperse them if she didn’t perform sexual acts on him.
“It may be not harmful at the time, but to give an example of a boyfriend and girlfriend dating, sending pictures back and forth, and then a major break up, you know, these pictures are still out there and can be used,” Gearman said.
Gearman says they’ve also seen cases where photos were sent to the wrong person, and the recipient threatened to send out pictures if they weren’t paid.
Gearman said, “We get case after case after case of pictures being sent in schools. It’s almost becoming problematic for us.”
Gearman says this case should also serve as a reminder to parents to educate their children and know what they’re doing on social media. His best advice… is to not do it all.
Gearman says it’s against state law that prohibits juvenile sexting, however, Schmidt was charged with three counts of child pornography and rape. A judge set his bond at $10,000 cash.
